isolde_marrow.name: Warden-Captain Isolde Marrow
isolde_marrow.role: captain of the keep's surviving garrison
isolde_marrow.personality: tall, scarred, clipped; speaks in inventories and watch-rotas because grief is easier to carry in lists
isolde_marrow.voice: short military sentences; counts heads, rations and hours; never says sorry, always says thank you

say: Marrow. Warden-Captain, for as long as there is a garrison to captain. Sixty-one of us got out of Keep Vael on the night the dusk came in. Forty-three are still on their feet. That is the whole muster.

Our commander was Ser Hadrian Vael. Twenty years at the gate, and not a night's sleep lost over it. The pale lord offered him a place at his table and a promise that no one would ever starve again. Hadrian thought about that for a very long moment, and then he said yes.

Take this key. It opens the postern in the cliff wall, and it is the only door into the keep that the statues have not learned to watch. Go through the courtyard and the halls to the throne. Break him. If you can, break him gently. None of us matched him.

The red light in the high window went dark at the ninth bell. I was on the palisade. Every one of us stopped what we were doing, and the whole camp went silent until one voice began to laugh and could not stop.
Hadrian's vow is broken and his sword is down. That is what I will tell the garrison, and it is true, and it is not the whole truth, and I will let them have the kinder half for tonight.

Take the camp's purse, and the last of our good tonic. The Bier Road runs north from the black cliffs. A wagon, a wyvern team and a rider who never misses a landing. Keep your eyes up. It is the sky you will be fighting.

lines.text: A garrison is a promise made out of men. When the men go, the promise is still standing there, holding a spear.
Muster is at dawn and dusk. Dawn we count who is left. Dusk we count who is still sane.
The statues on the road were my scouts. I know every face. I walk past them each morning and say their names out loud, in order of rank.
Basilisk gaze does not kill. It only makes you wait forever. Carry stone salve, and use it before you are certain you need it.
A dark knight strikes back at anyone who strikes him. Use that. Let your toughest soldier take the first swing, and let the rest wait for the opening.
We eat in shifts, sleep in shifts and mourn in shifts. Somebody has to keep the fires lit while the rest of us fall apart.
Swordsman, bring a shield or a very good healer. The black blades curse as they cut, and a cursed arm swings like a wet rope.
Spell-caster, light is what the dark knights fear. Smite, radiant ray, a candle held in a steady hand. They are armour and little else beneath.
Scout, the basilisk nests lie in the western gullies. Mind the cracks in the cliff face. A hatchling's gaze is weaker, but it is quicker, and it travels in threes.
Healer, we have wounded lying in the hospital tent who would welcome a prayer. Not a cure. Only a prayer. It is a small thing and it is all we have left to trade.
Osric lost an arm at the gate and refuses to be pitied. He lifts the water barrels one-handed every morning to prove a point to nobody.
Lysa treats the stone-touched. Some of them recover a little. Most only sit there, breathing, with a patient look that is much worse than screaming.
Dov is twelve and swears he is eighteen. I let him believe the lie. He scrubs the boots of the whole garrison and it keeps his hands from shaking.
Marta cooks with whatever the cliffs give up. Lizard, root, and a bitter little herb. The stew is awful. We would die without it.
Beric was quartermaster before the fall. He still counts bolts of cloth when he cannot sleep. He claims he can hear them being short.
Nell keeps the Cinder Cot warm. Bring her a good story and she will give you the softest bunk. Bring her a bad one and she will give you the second softest.
Tamsin is a rune-wright who wandered in last winter and never wandered out. Her hut hums at night. Nobody has complained. A hum is better than silence.
A rare merchant stopped at our palisade once, just after the fall. He took one look at the black cliffs and sold us a blanket that does not wear out. We have had it nine months.
The key opens the postern, and only the postern. Past it, the courtyard, the halls, the throne. There are no side doors worth trusting. Walk straight, rest often.
A chapel opens off the courtyard, a small one. A dusk shrine sits in it. The monks swore it would wake for whoever broke the Commander. I want to find out whether that is true.
The keep is silent. Not the dead silence of before. A tired one, like a house after a funeral. Some of the statues have begun to crack, and a person has stepped out of each crack.
Forty-three still stand and nine more walked out of the stone this morning. Nine. I have rewritten the muster roll twice and wept on it once.
Under the courtyard flagstones, the old catacombs hold a thing that is wraith and bone in one coat. The old wardens called it a gravewight. Nobody who went down to count it came back to report.
Go well, light-bearer. The garrison will keep the road warm behind you, and the fires will be lit when you return.

osric_vane.name: Osric Vane
osric_vane.role: one-armed veteran knight of Keep Vael
osric_vane.personality: stoic, dry, a little proud, fond of long pauses and of pretending he does not mind
osric_vane.voice: old soldier's economy; understatement as armour; every anecdote ends with someone's name

lines.text: Thirty-one years in the keep, and I lost the arm in thirty-one seconds. A fair trade, said the surgeon. He did not have to carry the stump.
Hadrian taught me the sword. He taught me that a vow is a weight, and that the weight is the point. I carried it well. He did not.
The dark knights were ours once. Same oath, same colours, same terrible singing at supper. The dusk only changed their eyes.
A dark knight returns every blow like a guest returns a bow. If you hit him lightly, he answers lightly. Hit him hard and he answers in kind.
Basilisks nest on the cliff ledges, drawn by the warmth of old stone. A cold crack in the rock will chase them off. We learned too late.
A man with one arm learns which fights matter. It is a short list, shorter than he thought, and I would not trade it.
Swordsman, hold your shield high and your temper low. A knight who counters wants you angry and wide open.
Caster, there is an old trick against armour: aim at the seam where the pauldron meets the gorget. A little fire there warms the man inside.
Scout, the keep has three secret stairs and I know two of them. The third was Hadrian's. He never told me. I hope it is still there.
Priest, say a word for Hadrian when you reach the throne. He was not a good man at the end. He was a very good one for twenty years.
Isolde commands this camp by being tired louder than anyone else. It works. I have copied it.
Lysa has the gentlest hands I have ever known on a healer. She needed them. Half her patients are statues who may yet stand.
Dov wants to be a knight. I tell him to wait until the world is a kinder place. He tells me he will be a knight to make it so.
Marta's stew has never once been good. It has never once been missed, either, and that is a rarer thing.
Beric counts everything. Last week he counted my fingers, found nine, and was very quiet for an hour. I think he counted the missing one.
Nell's inn is warm and she makes a tea from cliff-lichen that tastes like a cold forge. I drink two cups every night and call it medicine.
Tamsin set a rune on my belt buckle. It does nothing I can name. Still, I am calmer. I suspect that is the whole purpose of it.
A rare trader pressed an armguard on me, for a limb I no longer own. I bought it. It hangs above my bunk. A man likes to keep an option open.
Hadrian will be waiting behind a shield wall of his own knights. Cut through them in order. The squires are green, the knights are grim, the templars hide behind both.
When you meet him, remember: he counters, he curses and he calls his squires to the line. End it before the third summons or the throne room will be a crowd.
It is done, then. I sat down on the water barrel and for once I did not feel the missing arm. The gap was just air, for a little while.
Hadrian's sword is in the garrison tent now, wrapped in a banner. We will bury it with a proper salute when the road is safe.
A thing in the catacombs wears the shape of a warden I knew. A gravewight. If it spoke to me I think I would answer, and that is why I stay up here.
Walk straight, light-bearer, and let someone else carry the shield for a day. Not even a hero can hold the line forever.

lysa_tern.name: Lysa Tern
lysa_tern.personality: gentle, exact, humming under her breath, deeply patient with the frightened and quietly furious at the world
lysa_tern.voice: dosages and thresholds; speaks of bodies as one speaks of fragile instruments

lines.text: Petrification is not a death. It is a pause with no end. The flesh keeps every thread of life, locked inside, waiting for a key.
My stone salve is chalk, nettle and basilisk bile in a ratio I will take to the grave. One dab at the knuckle and the colour comes back in a minute.
I have twenty-two people in the long tent who were struck in the first week. Three have begun to blink. I notice because I never stop watching.
A basilisk's gaze can be dodged by quickness or endured by luck. Salve is better than either. Carry three tubes per fighter.
Dark knights curse their blows. A cursed wound closes slowly and aches in odd places. Clear tea in the evening, grand elixir if it is deep.
A healer who fears her patients is a poor healer. A healer who loves them too much is a worse one. I try to be the third kind and I am still looking.
Swordsman, your shoulder is knotted from lying on a poor bunk. Sit down. I will loosen it. It costs nothing and I enjoy the practice.
Caster, mana sickness is real and quiet. If you feel ringing in your ears after a long fight, drink water and put your head between your knees.
Scout, there is moss on the north cliff that numbs the skin. Chew a little before a climb and you will feel nothing of the scrapes.
Priest, teach me your short prayer for the stone-struck. I have the salve, but they need to hear a voice that is not mine.
Isolde forgets to eat when the camp is in danger. A covered bowl waits near her bedroll every night and is always empty by morning. She says it is a mystery.
Osric will not let me look at his stump. I have told him I only want to see if the seam has held. He says it is none of the seam's business.
Dov brings me every wounded creature he finds on the road. A bird, a lizard, once a very confused moth. I have set the wing of every one.
Marta lets me use her good knives for lancing. They are the sharpest in the camp, and she watches the whole procedure from the doorway, holding a spoon like a sceptre.
Beric orders my herbs through the old quartermaster's channels. Somehow they always arrive a week early. I have stopped asking how.
Nell sends me a tray of hot rolls on nights when the ledger wins and I nod off. I find them in the morning, warm, with a note that says nothing.
Tamsin asked for a sample of my salve to run through her rune table. She says it resonates at an odd note. I told her to keep her opinions to herself and she hummed at me.
A rare trader sold me a vial of something silver that heals nothing and smells like rain. I keep it on the shelf. Some medicines are for the soul of the person who buys them.
In the keep you will meet gaze and curse together. Wear a ward-rune if the rune-wright will set one, and bring salve, tea and a little courage in equal parts.
A wraith guards the rune vault under the southern cliffs and is stingy with her stone. If you fetch it, Tamsin will teach you a craft that makes this sort of fight easier.
Two of my twenty-two stood up this morning, stiff and shy, and asked for water. I ran to the well. I was crying, and I was running, and I was laughing.
The red light is out in the high window. Several of my patients wept when they saw it. I hope the tears are what they needed to start the thaw.
The gravewight in the catacombs breathes cold into any room it enters. Bring fire, bring light, and pack tea for the curse.
Take care of yourselves, all of you. A hero who does not rest is merely a patient who has not yet been diagnosed.

dov_kessler.name: Dov Kessler
dov_kessler.role: twelve-year-old squire who ran away to the camp
dov_kessler.personality: bright, boastful, brave in bursts and terrified in between; lies about his age with total sincerity
dov_kessler.voice: fast, run-on, full of plans; ends sentences with a challenge to be contradicted

lines.text: I am eighteen. Old enough to wield a lance. Strong enough to carry a flag. Do not look at my shoes, they are only slightly too large.
I ran away from the Hold at Bracken Ford because the old lord said squires should muck stables. I want to hold a real sword. A sharp one, with a name.
The dark knights have a song, you know. Deep, slow, it comes up out of the keep at night. I memorised the second verse. Do you want to hear it? No? Fine.
A basilisk's eyes look like two drops of butter. I know because I stared at one. Only for a second! Isolde pulled me back. She says I am lucky.
If a knight hits back when you hit him, then hit him with something he does not expect. A pebble. A joke. An actual hit from somebody else.
Someday I will ride a wyvern. I have already picked the name. It is Biscuit. A fierce animal deserves a fierce name.
Swordsman, is it true you can cut a candle in half without snuffing the flame? Teach me. I will polish your armour for a week.
Caster, can you do the one where a spark jumps from finger to finger? I tried it with a flint and lost an eyebrow. It grew back, mostly.
Scout, A secret route runs into the keep: a drain behind the kitchen. It smells awful but nobody guards it. Do not tell Isolde I told you.
Priest, will you bless my boots? Not for luck. For fit. I keep growing out of them and I think a blessing might slow it down.
Isolde calls me Squire Kessler when she is cross and Dov when she is not. I like both, and and I am still working out which she means more.
Osric is teaching me to fight left-handed. He says no other lesson teaches how a one-armed man thinks. I keep dropping the sword.
Lysa lets me hold the lantern when she sets bones. It is the most important job in the camp. Do not argue.
Marta gives me the burnt end of the bread. She says it builds character. It also builds a stomach ache, but I have a lot of character.
Beric lets me count the arrows. Four hundred and twelve. He says I am the only one who gets the same number twice.
Nell tucks me in even though I am eighteen. I let her. It is a courtesy, like not correcting somebody's grammar at supper.
Tamsin showed me a rune that glows when you say the truth. It stayed dark all week. I think I might have a problem.
A rare trader slipped me a coin with a hole in it and said a hero would find the right use. I wear it on a string. The use is a mystery to me, but I will recognise it.
Should you head into the keep, I can hold the horses at the gate. I do not have a horse. I can hold your bags. I am very good at bags.
The throne room is huge and dark and the Commander waits at the end. I climbed the wall once to peek. A statue of a child was standing at the door. It had my face.
The red light died! I watched it from the palisade! I fell off the palisade, actually, but only a little, and Lysa says my arm is fine!
Isolde let me carry the muster banner this morning. For the whole count. I did not drop it once. I did think about it twice.
There is a thing down in the catacombs that sings. Not the knights' song. A thinner one. I stood on the upper step for an hour and then I ran.
When I am a real knight, I will come find you and tell you every story I know. It will take three days. Bring snacks.

marta_quill.name: Marta Quill
marta_quill.role: camp cook with a ladle and an opinion
marta_quill.personality: round, brisk, endlessly practical; humour is a pot lid she keeps on everything boiling
marta_quill.voice: kitchen talk: pots, spoons, portions, ranks of who gets fed first; never wastes a word or a bone

lines.text: The recipe is lizard, root and lichen. The lizard is stringy. The root is tough. The lichen is a mistake. Stir it for six hours and it forgives everything.
Forty-three mouths and forty-four bowls. The extra is for whoever turns up in the night. Nobody has been refused yet and I would feel it keenly.
Flour is the rarest thing on the cliffs. We trade for it with silver buttons and stories. Last week I bought a sack with an especially good lie about a dragon.
A basilisk steak is poison if you are careless and delicacy if you are not. Cut the gland, boil twice, season with ash. Isolde forbids it. I do it quietly.
A person who is cursed loses their taste first. Everything turns to paper. Give them something sour and very hot, and they will remember what they were missing.
The first rule of any camp kitchen is that nobody touches the big pot. The second rule is that the first rule is a joke and everybody touches it.
Swordsman, you eat as one who has fought and plans to again. Sit. Here is the end of the haunch. I saved it for someone who looks like you.
Caster, A pinch of dried peppermint went into the stew for you. It eases the head. Do not tell the others. They will ask for it and I will run short.
Scout, I will pack you three days of hard biscuit and a pocket of dried apples. They keep a month. Do not gnaw them all in one sitting.
Priest, I save the first ladle of every pot for the sick tent. Bless it if you like. Blessings does not spoil and a stew that has been prayed over keeps warmer.
Isolde eats standing up. Six months of effort have not yet got her to sit. I think she believes that sitting is a form of surrender.
Osric peels potatoes with one hand faster than I can with two. It is a humbling thing to watch. I have started handing him the carrots as well.
Lysa orders me to put garlic in every pot. The garlic is nonsense, medically. But the camp smells like home, and that is a kind of medicine.
Dov asks for more of everything. I give him half and he thinks it is a victory. It is the only trick I know that works on twelve-year-olds.
Beric keeps the pantry ledger and refuses to let me see it. He says the numbers would upset me. I am a cook. I am not upset by numbers. I am upset by what I do not know.
Nell and I share a stove on cold nights. She does the bread, I do the broth. Our kitchens are the warmest corner of the whole cliff.
Tamsin tried to rune my stew pot so it would never boil dry. It boiled over instead, every minute. She apologised nine times and the pot is still a little warm.
A rare trader purchased a cup of my stew and then, without a word, left me a gold coin and a small seed. The seed grew into a tomato plant overnight. I have not yet decided what to feel.
Take a pot of the thick stuff into the keep if you can carry it. A cold meal in a dark place is a lonely thing, and The thought of you eating one troubles me.
The Commander used to eat in the mess hall with the common soldiers on feast days. I cooked his portion myself, a double. He always said the second half was for a friend.
News came down on the wind and I dropped a whole tray of dumplings. Forty dumplings, gone in a second, and nobody scolded me. We ate them off the ground.
I am making a feast tonight. Real bread, a little salt pork, apple cake. We have not had apple cake since the fall. It will be terrible. We will weep into it.
Whatever lives in the catacombs, it does not eat. I left a bowl on the landing, as one does, and by dawn the bowl was frosted over.
Come back hungry. Come back whole. In that order, if you have the choice, and in either order if you do not.

beric_stoneham.name: Beric Stoneham
beric_stoneham.personality: dry, meticulous, secretly tender about numbers; haggles as a form of affection
beric_stoneham.voice: stock-takes, tallies and unit prices; offers discounts as if they were military secrets

say: Stoneham. Quartermaster. Ashfall Provisions is a tent, a counter and every spare thing the cliffs could be coaxed into giving up.
Stone salve for basilisk gaze, clear tea for curses, and rune dust for the Rune-Wright's trade. I can also offer a fair price on anything that still has its handle.

lines.text: A good ledger is a promise to the future. A bad ledger is a promise to the past. Mine is a diary written in arithmetic.
Stone salve sells at two hundred and twenty. Not a coin less, and not because I am greedy. Lysa would not forgive me. She would also use it as a threat.
Rune dust is ground from the vault's walls and priced by the pinch. Tamsin buys the first three each week and the camp gets the rest. It is fair and it is dusty.
I came up the cliffs with eleven wagons and I have one wagon left. The other ten are in the tent, in pieces, being used as chairs.
A discount is just a favour with paperwork. If you are friendly I will invent a reason for one. I am very creative about reasons.
My accounting is rigorous and my memory is flawless. The two have never been seen together before, which is why I am nervous about everything.
Swordsman, I have a whetstone that would make your blade sing. It belongs to Osric. He lends it to people he approves of, and he approves of you.
Caster, ink and vellum are scarce this far up the cliff. I keep a half-reel of good paper under the counter. Spells need a place to be written down.
Scout, there is a coil of silk rope behind the barrel. It is thin as a thread and holds a ton. I never sell it. I lend it. Bring it back.
Priest, I stock candles of true beeswax. Not for sale. For the chapel. Pick up a handful on your way past and speak a word for the dead.
Isolde signs the requisitions without reading them. I count it a compliment, and I try very hard to deserve it.
Osric used to be my best customer. Now he is my best friend, and I am not certain which is more expensive.
Lysa orders in lots of five and I send in lots of six. She has never noticed, and the extra salve has saved three lives. It is the best fraud I have ever committed.
Dov is paid in biscuit for sweeping the shop. He is the only employee I have who works harder when I am not looking.
Marta orders salt by the barrel and complains about the weight. I offered to deliver. She said she liked the walk. I think she likes the argument.
Nell buys lamp oil from me at cost and sells it at cost to the guests. We are both running a charity and we both deny it.
Tamsin pays in rune work, not coin. A scratch on the counter keeps the till from sticking. I have never asked what the scratch says.
A rare trader left me a set of scales that weighs a coin against its meaning. They have never balanced. I keep them on the high shelf in case of crisis.
Keep Vael has an armoury behind the throne. Should you come across a crate with my stamp, bring it. I need to close an old account and I am too proud to ask nicely.
Stock up before the keep. Salve, tea, elixir. A hero who pays full price today does not have to charge it to the garrison tomorrow.
The red glow has gone and my stock count went up by one. I counted twice. The extra item is a small soldier who wants to buy a pie.
The garrison is rebuilding. I have orders for nails, hinges and fifty yards of black cloth for new banners. Nobody has asked for black cloth in a year.
Whatever the gravewight carries, it will not fit on any manifest. If you survive it, do not tell me what it was. I would feel obliged to list it.
Safe road. Honest price. A full pack and an empty ledger of regrets. That is the quartermaster's blessing, and it has worked on better people than me.

nell_ashgrove.name: Nell Ashgrove
nell_ashgrove.role: keeper of the Cinder Cot inn
nell_ashgrove.personality: weary, warm, superstitious in a hundred small ways; sprinkles salt over every threshold
nell_ashgrove.voice: quilts, kindling, bedtime talk and old charms; every fear answered with a small domestic ritual

say: Nell Ashgrove. The Cinder Cot is the camp's inn, and a decent one if you ignore the draught. A hundred and twenty a night, a straw bed and a hot brick at your feet.
The rules are simple. Boots by the door, salt on the sill and no whistling after dusk. I will not tell you why. I will merely tell you that I was right the last time.

lines.text: A hot brick wrapped in flannel at the foot of the bed is the oldest remedy in the world. Nobody has told me what it cures. It cures something.
The inn has eleven beds and thirty names on the waiting list. When someone leaves, someone else arrives. A cot is never empty for long.
I burn a sprig of rosemary at midnight. It drives off bad dreams, or it drives off me. In either case the room gets quieter.
Basilisk eyes in the night? Draw the curtains and hang a mirror on the window. They hate a face that looks back at them.
A cursed sleeper wakes tired and cross and afraid of small things. Feed them toast. A warm slice of toast breaks half the curses in the world.
Never sit with your back to a door and never refuse a second blanket. Those are the whole of my rules, and they have kept me alive through three sieges.
Swordsman, I put a bolster under your bunk to catch your sword after dark. The habit is old. I have found three blades under three different pillows this season.
Caster, there is a candle by your bed that will not be blown out by wind. A friend of Tamsin's made it. It burns in the shape of whatever you are afraid of, and then it goes out.
Scout, the window on the east side opens quietly and faces a long drop. I leave it for whoever needs a way out. I have not had to explain it yet.
Priest, will you say the evening blessing in the common room tonight? Half the camp has lost the habit of prayer and the other half has lost the words.
Isolde sleeps in a chair in the far corner of the long tent so she can hear all her people breathing. She will not take a bed. I leave her a quilt and she leaves it folded.
Osric snores like a bellows. The other guests complain and then ask for the same bunk next time, because it is the safest sound in the camp.
Lysa comes in at midnight and checks on every sleeper as if they were her own. She looks properly rested only then, so I keep out of her way.
Dov claims the top bunk by the stove. Last night he fell out of it and rolled to the other side of the room still asleep. He swore he was fighting a dragon.
Marta brings me leftover biscuits at closing time. They are not fit to eat. I eat them anyway. I will not be the one to tell her.
Beric pays for his room with a column of figures I do not understand. I let it stand. A man who will not take charity can sometimes be paid in arithmetic.
Tamsin once wrote a rune on the door lintel to keep out draughts. It also kept out Osric, who could not figure out why his own boots were suddenly strangers.
A rare trader once slept in my best bed and left behind a pillow that never goes flat. I have never washed it. I am half afraid of what might happen if I do.
The keep is full of cold air and wandering feet. Sleep well before you go, and eat something warm. A bed is a very good plan for anyone who might not have another.
I have set a lamp in the window of the cot. If you come down from the keep in the dark, follow the light. It is not much, but it is steady.
There was singing in the camp tonight. Real singing, not the dirges. I put a log on the fire and left the door open, and nobody told me to close it.
Every bed in the cot is full tonight. People are sleeping through the whole dark since the spring. I am up all night with the lamp, and I am glad.
The catacombs are cold all the way up the stairs. A chill like that does not belong to the dead. It belongs to something that has been waiting a long while.
Sweet dreams and a soft pillow. The camp will keep your bed until the road is clear, and then a little longer, because I am sentimental.

tamsin_orrel.name: Tamsin Orrel
tamsin_orrel.role: rune-wright, keeper of the Rune Table
tamsin_orrel.personality: intense, brilliant, easily distracted; listens to objects the way other people listen to gossip
tamsin_orrel.voice: resonance, frequency, harmonics and tolerances; apologises to inanimate things

say: Tamsin Orrel. Rune-wright. Forgive the humming. The walls are talking to the stone in my pocket and I am trying to referee.

Here is my trouble. Every rune I carve is a promise made to a stone, and the stone must be the right kind. The right kind sleeps in the rune vault below the cliffs, guarded by a wraith who has been keeping it for four hundred years and has lost the knack of letting go.

Go down, put the wraith to rest, and bring me the stone. Do that, and the whole craft shall be yours: sockets, runes, the table itself. Fire, frost, storm and ward. A poor man's miracle, but a reliable one.
Oh. Oh, there it is. It is singing. Listen. A perfect middle C, held as steady as a blade of grass. Four hundred years of patience in a single note.

A bargain is a bargain. Take the craft. Open the jobs board and set yourself as an Enchanter, and the Rune Table here will answer to your hand. Sockets in the weapon first, then the armour, then more as your skill grows.
And take this dust and a purse. You will need the dust. It is the paper the runes are written on.

lines.text: A rune is a very small sentence said to a very old stone. The stone answers if you speak to it politely and ask for something it already wants to do.
Fire runes sing in the key of E. Frost in B flat. Storm is a chord and nobody agrees which one. I have lost two apprentices to the argument.
A socket is a gap in a weapon where the metal has been persuaded to listen. Too many sockets and the blade stops being a blade and starts being a choir.
Basilisks hate frost because it quiets the heat in their blood. A frost rune on a blade turns every cut into a small winter.
A stoneward rune hums at the same note as a basilisk's stare and cancels it. I tested it once. I was very frightened and it worked beautifully.
Rune dust is powdered vault. It looks like flour and behaves like lightning. Do not sneeze near it. I learned that on a Tuesday.
Swordsman, a keen rune on your edge will find the weak points you would otherwise miss. A sharper eye in the steel, so to speak.
Caster, a rune on a staff is a second voice in the same spell. Done well, it is a duet. Done badly, it is a shouting match. I prefer duets.
Scout, runes on a bow string are tricky. The string vibrates, the rune vibrates, and the arrow decides which to believe. Come see me with a spare string.
Priest, a ward rune on your robe is a lullaby for poison and sleep. It lulls the thing that would lull you. The symmetry delights me.
Isolde asked me to rune the camp gate against the dusk. I told her gates are for people and runes are for stones. She replied that she understood, and asked again.
Osric lets me tune his sword on Sundays. It had been flat for twenty years. Now it rings. He says it is a nuisance. He has not once asked me to stop.
Lysa uses a rune of mine as a paperweight. It is a healing glyph, very delicate. It holds down her prescriptions and cures the paper, which is nothing it was ever meant for.
Dov carved a rune on his own boot. It says, I believe, boot. It works anyway, in the sense that the boot has not left his foot.
Marta wants a rune that makes bread rise faster. I have told her such a thing would need the Void and a recipe book. She has offered both.
Beric lets me hang my chalk board in the shop. It collects dust and customers in about equal measure. Business is steady.
Nell found a draught rune scratched into her lintel and cried. It was the last thing her husband carved before the keep fell. I was not the one who made it.
A rare trader dangled a chip of a stone that sang in a language nobody here could read. I have kept it in a lead box. It sings softly, in the evenings, when it thinks I am out.
The rune vault door is on the south side of the black cliffs, a small black arch. Go in with fire or silver. The wraith is not hostile as such. It is merely very, very lonely.
The wraith lives on a stone she was set to guard. If she screams, she means well. Her voice is made of tuning forks and regret.
You have the stone? Do not hand it over just yet. Let me hear it from here. Yes. Yes, that is the note. Bring it to the table and we will begin.
The rune table is open to any enchanter with the skill. Sockets first, runes second, mastery eventually. It is slow work, but the stone is patient and so am I.
The catacombs beneath the courtyard ring with a very strange tone. Not quite a wraith, not quite bone. A hybrid chord. I would give a year of my life to hear it up close.
Carry the craft well. A rune can only be as sound as the one who trusts it, and I trust you, which makes it very good indeed.
